title: Care and Maintenance
summary: Clothes get dirty with dirt, grease and perspiration and lose strength and appearance, so they must be cared for. Laundering means washing, drying and finishing of clothes; dry cleaning cleans without water using solvents and grease absorbents. Steps in laundering: mending (tears, loose buttons), stain removal (before washing, or stains spread and fix), sorting (by fibre type: cotton, wool, silk, synthetics; whites separate from coloured; very dirty separate), soaking (loosens dirt; not for non-fast colours and not for woollens, which felt), washing, rinsing (2–4 times until all soap is removed), starching and bluing, drying (whites in sun, coloured in shade, silk in shade, synthetics on a hanger in shade, woollens flat in shade) and ironing and pressing (cotton damp with a hot iron, silk damp, synthetics and rayon moderately hot, woollens over damp muslin).

A detergent is a cleansing product: a soap (from natural oil, fat and waxes) or a syndet (synthetic, from chemicals). Both lower the surface tension of water. Syndets wet the fabric more readily, dissolve in hot and cold water, work in hard water (soaps foam well only in soft water), smell sweet, already have blues and optical brightening agents, leave no deposits (soap leaves soapy deposits that make clothes dull) and are more economical in the long run, though soaps are cheaper. Auxiliaries are products other than cleansers that give a good finish: blues, optical brightening agents, chemical bleaches, stain-removing agents and stiffening agents (starch gives a crisp finish). Blue counteracts yellowness of white cottons and linens; apply just before the last rinse after mixing thoroughly (ultramarine and Prussian blue). Optical brightening agents (OBA or FBA) are colourless fluorescent dyes that absorb ultraviolet light and reflect visible light, making clothes whiter; no chemical action. Chemical bleaches whiten by oxidising or reducing action. Oxidising bleaches (almost permanent; for cotton and linen): sunlight (the oldest, simplest; wet the stain and put it on grass), Javelle water (sodium hypochlorite; dilute and rinse well), potassium permanganate with oxalic acid (brown stains such as rust, paan, dyes, mildew, perspiration and ink) and hydrogen peroxide (universal bleach for animal and vegetable fibres; store in dark bottles). Reducing bleaches (milder; for wool and silk, which may turn yellow again): sodium hydrosulphite and sodium bisulphite.

A stain is a mark other than dirt. Identify by colour, smell and feel (curry and pickle yellow; tea and coffee brown; grass green; paint and sugar syrup stiff; lipstick and shoe polish slippery). Categories: vegetable (curry, tea, coffee), animal (milk, blood), grease (butter, shoe polish), mineral (rust), grass and miscellaneous (dyes). Methods: dipping, sponging, drop method and steaming. Precautions: treat stains fresh, know the fabric, identify the stain, start with simple methods and wash with cold water first for protein stains like blood and egg (hot water coagulates them), test chemicals on a small portion, repeated mild reagents are better than one strong one, wash with soapy solution at the end and dry in the sun. Examples: fresh tea or coffee on white cotton: pour boiling water; old: glycerine and sodium perborate or hydrogen peroxide; coloured cotton: soak in warm water with borax; fresh blood: wash with cold water and soap; old blood: salt water (2 tablespoons in half a bucket); fresh curry or butter: hot water and soap or talcum powder; paint, shoe polish, nail polish, lipstick and ball pen: rub with spirit or kerosene; grass: soap and water, old: methylated spirit; paan: paste of onion; mehndi: warm milk; rust: lime juice and salt.

Choice depends on how dirty and what fabric. Friction washing (strong cottons: by hand, with a plastic brush for very soiled things like dusters, or beating with a stick for large articles); suction washing (heavy pile fabrics such as towels, with a suction washer creating a vacuum); kneading and squeezing (delicate silks, woollens and rayon; gentle, no change of shape); machine washing. Wool: no soaking, lukewarm water, light pressure, liquid soap or reetha solution (not for whites), dry flat. Silk: no soaking, lukewarm water. Synthetics: lukewarm or cold water, no hot water as they melt. Storage: empty pockets and brush, sun and air worn clothes, do not let them get too dirty, never store damp clothes (mildew), and protect from insects with tobacco, dried neem, camphor and moth balls; woollens packed in newspaper because moths dislike printer's ink.

objective: In your laundry room you find four laundry powders A, B, C and D with these functions. Powder A: makes white clothes appear brighter when dried in sunlight. Powder B: eliminates yellow tints when added just before the final rinse. Powder C: safely removes stains from both silk and cotton. Powder D: gives cotton clothes a crisp, stiff finish and helps them resist dirt. Identify these powders.
A: optical brightening agent (OBA). B: blue (fabric whitener). C: hydrogen peroxide (a universal bleach). D: starch (stiffening agent).
Give a material or reagent for each stain. (a) Tea or coffee on cotton (b) Blood stain (c) Grass stain (old) (d) Paan stain.
(a) Borax or boiling water. (b) Cold salted water. (c) Methylated spirit. (d) A paste of onion.

State True or False. (a) Woollen clothes should be soaked before washing. (b) White clothes should be dried in shade. (c) Optical brightening agents are colourless dyes. (d) Silks should be washed by kneading and squeezing.
(a) False: they felt when soaked. (b) False: whites are dried in the sun. (c) True. (d) True.

Give one word. (a) A collective name for white petrol, methylated spirit and benzene (b) A chemical used as a fabric whitener (c) A cleanser produced synthetically from chemicals (d) A natural oxidising bleach.
(a) Volatile (dry cleaning) solvents. (b) Blue. (c) Syndet. (d) Sunlight.
You find a grass stain on your white cotton shirt. What should you do first and why?
Wash it with soap and cold water first if it is fresh. If it is old, dip the stain in methylated spirit because it dissolves the chlorophyll stain.
vsa: Your friend spilled fresh curry on her white cotton kurta. Suggest two immediate steps she should take to remove the stain.
Apply talcum powder on the fresh stain and leave it for a few hours, then brush it off. Wash with hot water and soap and dry in the sun.
Give one reason each for the statements. (i) Woollen clothes should not be soaked before washing. (ii) Clothes should not be stored when damp. (iii) Blood stains should be removed with cold water.
(i) Soaking leads to felting of wool. (ii) Moisture causes mildew. (iii) Hot water coagulates blood proteins and fixes the stain.
Why is vinegar sometimes added to the final rinse for silks? Why are woollens packed in newspapers?
Vinegar removes soap traces and keeps silk bright. Newspaper ink repels moths.
What is laundering? Name its steps in order (any five).
Laundering is washing, drying and finishing of clothes. The steps are mending, stain removal, sorting, soaking, washing, rinsing, starching or bluing, drying and ironing.
Name two differences between a soap and a syndet.
A soap is made from natural oil or fat; a syndet is made synthetically from chemicals. Syndets work in hard water and leave no deposits; soaps foam well only in soft water.
What are auxiliaries in laundering? Give two examples.
Products other than cleansers that give a good finish are auxiliaries. Blues and optical brightening agents are examples.
sa: Explain the precautions to be taken while removing stains (three points).

(i) Remove the stain when fresh and identify the fabric and the stain. (ii) Wash first with cold water (hot coagulates blood and egg) and use mild chemicals, trying them on a small portion first. (iii) Wash with soap solution at the end to remove chemicals and dry in the sun.
Distinguish between oxidising and reducing bleaches (three points).

(i) Oxidising bleaches have an almost permanent effect and are used on cotton and linen (sunlight, Javelle water, hydrogen peroxide). (ii) Reducing bleaches are milder and used on wool and silk (sodium hydrosulphite). (iii) Wool and silk bleached with reducing bleaches may turn yellow again in air.
Explain the precautions for storing clothes (three points).
(i) Brush clothes and sun and air them before storing. (ii) Never store damp or very dirty clothes. (iii) Protect against insects with neem, camphor or moth balls and pack woollens in newspaper.
Explain the different methods of washing and the fabrics suited to each.

(i) Friction washing (by hand, brush or beating) for strong cottons. (ii) Suction washing for heavy pile fabrics such as towels. (iii) Kneading and squeezing for delicate silk, wool and rayon, and machine washing for large loads.
How will you wash woollen clothes? (three points)

(i) Do not soak them; use lukewarm water and mild liquid soap or reetha solution (not for whites). (ii) Use light pressure and kneading and squeezing. (iii) Rinse well and dry flat in shade; press with a damp muslin.
la: Explain the steps in laundering of clothes.

(i) Mending tears and loose buttons and removing stains before washing. (ii) Sorting by fibre, colour and degree of dirt. (iii) Soaking to loosen dirt (not for woollens or non-fast colours). (iv) Washing with soap or syndet by a suitable method, then rinsing till all soap goes. (v) Starching and bluing as required. (vi) Drying (whites in sun, coloured in shade, woollens flat) and ironing according to the fabric.
